extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, proofreaders, compositors, and typesetters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical style and typesetting rules for punctuation, hyphenation, word division, footnotes, indexing, and tables for academic/technical publishing. Covers general principles and language-specific division rules for setting and proofreading text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Brackets are used (i) to inclose an explanation or note, (2) to indicate an interpolation in a quotation, (3) to rectify a mistake, (4) to supply an omission, and (5) for parentheses within parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each use (editorial notes in brackets, interpolations such as [the free-silver Democrats], rectifications like [Englishman], supplying omitted bibliographic info in brackets, and using brackets for nested parentheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicating continued material with brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'To be continued' at the end and 'Continued from ...' at the beginning of articles/chapters should be placed between brackets, centered, set in italics, and in reduced type per rules governing reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: [Continued from p. 320] and [To be concluded]; see cross-references to type-size reduction rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipses: when and how to use
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses indicate omission from a quotation of words not essential to the conveyed idea, illegible words, mutilations, or lacunae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For an ellipsis at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence, ordinarily use four periods separated by a space (en-quad). If the preceding line ends in a point, do not include that point among the four. When whole paragraphs/lines are omitted, insert a full line of periods separated by em- or 2-em quads according to line length, but do not extend beyond the longest type-line. Examples given in prose and poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis as part of citation
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipsis should be treated as part of the citation and therefore enclosed in the quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to bracket/quotation guidance (see 178[3]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen: general placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A hyphen is placed at the end of a line terminating with a syllable of a word carried to the next line, and between many compound words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See divisions section for rules governing line-break hyphenation; hyphen also used between components of many compounds (with many subrules below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives before a noun
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate two or more words (except proper names forming a unity) combined into one adjective preceding a noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: so-called Croesus, well-known author, first-class investment, better-trained teachers, nineteenth-century progress, up-to-date machinery, four-year-old boy; exceptions noted (e.g., New Testament times).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use en-dash for certain compounds set in capitals or with multiword components
rubrics_metrics.description: Where such words are set in capitals (e.g., headlines), or where one component contains more than one word, use an en-dash in place of a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: FRANCO-PRUSSIAN WAR; New York–Chicago freight traffic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not hyphenate adjectives formed with -ly adverbs or postpositive adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not connect by a hyphen adjectives or participles with adverbs ending in '-ly', nor such combinations when following the noun or qualifying a predicate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: highly developed species; a man well known in the neighborhood; 'Her gown and carriage were strictly up to date.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate noun compounds in objective relation
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, hyphenate nouns formed by combining two nouns where one component is derived from a transitive verb (objective relation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: mind-reader, story-teller, office-holder, property-owner, hero-worship. Exceptions: common brief compounds like lawgiver, taxpayer, proofreader, bookkeeper, stockholder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate present participle + noun formations
rubrics_metrics.description: A present participle united with a noun to form a new noun with a distinctive meaning, or with a preposition used absolutely, should have a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: boarding-house, dining-hall, sleeping-room, walking-stick, working-man; note phrasing 'the putting-in or taking-out of a hyphen.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of book/house/mill/room/shop/work: hyphenation by syllable-count
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'book', 'house', 'mill', 'room', 'shop', and 'work' are printed as one word when the prefixed noun contains one syllable, hyphenated when it contains two, and printed as two words when it contains three or more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: handbook, schoolbook, notebook; pocket-book, story-book; reference book. boathouse, clubhouse vs engine-house, power-house; commill, handmill vs chocolate mill; bedroom, classroom vs lecture-room; tinshop, workshop vs policy shop, handwork; exceptions include rare combinations and appearances where separation is better: source-book, wheat-mill, school work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of maker/dealer and occupations usually hyphenated
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'maker', 'dealer', and other occupation words should ordinarily be hyphenated; nouns denoting different occupations of the same individual likewise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harness-maker, book-dealer, job-printer; a soldier-statesman, poet-artist Rossetti. Exceptions: short everyday words like bookmaker, dressmaker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'store' hyphenation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'store' should be hyphenated when the prefix contains only one syllable; otherwise not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: drug-store, feed-store (but bookstore); grocery store, dry-goods store.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'fellow' and familial relation words
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'fellow' are always hyphenated; compounds of 'father', 'mother', 'brother', 'sister', 'daughter', 'parent', and 'foster' should be hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fellow-man, fellow-being; father-love (but fatherland), mother-tongue, brother-officer, sister-nation, foster-son.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate 'great-' for degrees of descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'great', indicating the fourth degree in direct line of descent, call for a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: great-grandfather, great-grandson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds of 'life' and 'world'
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'life' and 'world' require a hyphen in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: life-history, life-principle (but lifetime), world-power, world-problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation rules for 'skin' compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'skin' with words of one syllable are printed as one word; with words of more than one syllable, as two separate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: calfskin, sheepskin; alligator skin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compounds of 'master' and 'god' hyphenation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compounds of 'master' should be hyphenated; compounds of 'god' are hyphenated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: master-builder, master-stroke (exception: masterpiece). sun-god, rain-god.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation with fractional numbers spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: In fractional numbers spelled out, connect numerator and denominator by a hyphen unless either already contains a hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'two-thirds', 'four-and-five-sevenths', 'thirty-hundredths'; exceptions like 'one half' construction where hyphenation isn't used in prose contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use hyphen to indicate omitted common element of series
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more compound words occurring together share a component that is omitted from all but the last word, indicate the omission by hyphen(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English- and German-speaking countries; one-, five-, and ten-cent pieces. Note some consider this style Teutonism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphen to indicate incomplete prefix or suffix and syllabification
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a hyphen to indicate a prefix or suffix not complete in itself (e.g., 'The prefix a-') and to show syllables of a word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The prefix a-'; 'di-a-gram', 'pho-tog-ra-phy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of common hyphenated everyday words
rubrics_metrics.description: A set list of everyday-occurrence words that should be hyphenated, not covered by prior classifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples listed include after-years, cross-section, man-of-war, son-in-law, bas-relief, death-rate, page-proof, title-page, common-sense, post-office, well-being, cross-reference, horse-power, sense-perception, will-power, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary word divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid all unnecessary divisions of words; where consistent with good spacing, carry the whole word to the next line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General admonition; see specific limits below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide very short words; guidance by word-length
rubrics_metrics.description: In wide measures (20 ems or more), do not divide on a syllable of two-letter words; words of four letters should never be divided; words of five or six letters rarely divided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'only' should not be divided as on-ly; 'occur' rarely divided as oc-cur; priority of good spacing over forced division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit consecutive lines ending in hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Never let more than two consecutive lines terminate in a hyphen if avoidable; avoid a divided word at the next-to-last line and ensure the last line ('breakline') contains at least four letters in measures of 15 ems and up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also avoid a divided word at the bottom of a recto page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not divide proper nouns or separate initials/abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not divide proper nouns unless absolutely necessary; do not separate initials of a name or combinations like a.d., P.M., etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry initials and such combinations together on one line where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep divisional marks with the material they precede
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid separating a divisional mark (e.g., (a) or (i)) from the section it precedes; do not allow such marks to fall at the end of a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carry the mark over with the matter to which it pertains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide according to pronunciation (American system)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide words according to pronunciation rather than derivation (contrast with English system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: democ-racy not demo-cracy; knowledge not knowl-edge; auriferous not auri-ferous. However, where compatible with pronunciation and spacing, divide compounds on etymological lines: dis-pleasure better than displeas-ure; school-master rather than schoolmas-ter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division between consonants and vowel rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When two consonants meet between vowels and the syllable ends on one consonant, division may be made between the consonants; divide on a vowel wherever practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ad-van-tage, exces-sive, finan-cier; avoid terminating a line in a soft 'c' or soft 'g' when possible (divide to keep pronunciation and spelling intact). Exceptions: words in -able and -ible should carry the vowel over into the next line (read-able, convert-ible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid additional hyphens in hyphenated nouns/adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: In hyphenated nouns and adjectives avoid creating additional hyphens through division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: object-lesson, not object-les-son; fellow-being, not fel-low-being; poverty-stricken, not pover-ty-stricken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat diphthongs as one letter when dividing
rubrics_metrics.description: A coalition of two vowel sounds into one (a diphthong) should be treated as one letter; avoid dividing across the diphthong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: people and Caesar should not be divided as peo-ple or Cae-sar if alternative divisions cause awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of derivatives when accent shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: In derivatives from words ending in an accented syllable, the accented syllable should be carried into the next line with the suffix if the accent has been shifted; if derivative retains accent, leave the accented part in the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: objec-tive (from ob'ject) vs defect-ive (from defect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Plural s does not justify new division
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a plural 's' (creating a new syllable) does not justify dividing the word differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of impossible divisions: hor-ses and circumstan-ces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide adjectives in -ical on the 'i'
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjectives ending in -ical should be divided on the 'i' (physi-cal rather than phys-ical or physic-al).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short admonition: 'Do not divide nothing.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: French
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental principle: divide on a vowel as far as possible, avoiding consonantal endings of syllables; specific rules about consonant clusters and mute 'e'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative divisions: in-di-vi-si-bi-li-te, a-che-ter; two-consonant rules (ta-bleau not tab-leau); mute e not forming syllable in some cases (e-taient, joue-rai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: German
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; if several consonants stand between vowels, usually carry only the last over; certain consonant combinations (sz, ch, sch, ph, st, th) are never separated; ck divides as k-k if needed; carry certain consonant clusters in foreign words; compound words separated first into components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: hi-ten, le-ben; Rit-ter, Klemp-ner; Busche, Be-cher (but Haus-chen exception); Deckel—Dek-kel; Fürsten-schloss, Tür-an-gel, Inter-esse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: Italian
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; s before consonant, r after consonant, ch, gh, gli, gn, qu, sc, etc., are never separated; certain vowel combinations are not separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ta-vo-ll-no, nar-ra-re; ca-sti-ghi, in-chio-stro; miei, tu6i (liaison rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: Spanish
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide on a vowel as far as possible; ch, ll, rr and ñ considered simple consonants; cc and nn divided as in English; liquid consonants l and r should not be separated from preceding consonant except in compounds; two separable consonants should be divided; s always disjoined from following consonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ca-ra-co-les, mu-cha-cho, ci-ga-rro; sub-lu-nar exception; cuer-da, chas-co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: Greek
rubrics_metrics.description: Place single consonants, consonant combinations able to begin a word, and mutes followed by liquids at beginning of syllable; other consonant combinations are divided; compound words separated first into original parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include transliterated Greek syllabifications and compound separations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-language division rules: Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: Latin words have as many syllables as vowels/diphthongs; divide before a single consonant between vowels; divide before the last consonant when multiple consonants occur, with exceptions for mute+liquid and qu/gu; compound words separated into component elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cae-sar, me-ri-di-es, om-nis, scrip-tus, ad-est, red-e-o.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnote indices: use of superior figures and alternative symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use superior figures for reference indices as a rule; only in special cases (e.g., tables or algebraic matter) employ asterisks, daggers, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence when not using figures: * (asterisk), † (dagger), ‡ (double dagger), § (section mark), || (parallels), ¶ (paragraph mark). Place index figures in the text after punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'ibid.' and repeated references
rubrics_metrics.description: Where references to the same work follow closely and uninterruptedly, use 'ibid.' instead of repeating the title. 'Ibid.' takes the place of as much of the previous reference as is repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ordinarily use 'ibid.' for the first footnote on a verso page; better to repeat the title if short or use loc. cit. or op. cit. Examples shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes to tables formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes to tables should be in 6-pt. type and placed at the foot of the table (not the page). Use asterisks etc. for table reference indices, not superior figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to general footnote index guidance; see note on table formatting and type sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit abbreviations in references unless necessary; punctuation for classical references
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily omit 'Vol.', 'chap.', and 'p.' in references to particular passages; use Roman numerals for Volume, Book, Part, Division (capitals) and lower-case roman for chapter and introductory matter; use Arabic numerals for issue and text pages. For classical references, use periods in place of commas for divisions and omit the comma after the author's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for modern and classical references; use parentheses for date after volume in periodical references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number footnotes consecutively through an article/chapter for linotype
rubrics_metrics.description: In work set on the linotype machine, number footnotes consecutively through an article (in a journal) or through a chapter (in a book) to save resetting in case of changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note exceptions for specific journals which have their own styles (Botanical Gazette, Astrophysical Journal, Classical Philology, Classical Journal). Examples of those journals' styles provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing names: particles, prefixes, and hyphenation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for alphabetizing names and firms: French/Belgian/Spanish names with particles ('le','la','l','du','des') listed under prefix before ordinary L/D; 'de' or 'd'' under the first letter of the following word with the particle placed after initials; if the particle is part of surname index under particle (De Bey); German 'von' names indexed under the main name following 'von'; names beginning with M', Mac, Mc with following letter capitalized listed in advance of ordinary M list and ordered by letters after 'M', otherwise natural M order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: names preceded by O', St., Van with following capitalized placed in advance of O, S, or V lists; names with 'and/&/y/et/und/e' indexed under the first name; hyphenated names listed according to name following hyphen if English, preceding if French; German names with umlaut indexed as if base vowel; cross-references guidance pointer to other rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabular work: type sizes and setting rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance for type sizes and leading for open and ruled tables depending on main matter point-size: in 11-pt and 10-pt matter open tables ordinarily set in 9-pt leaded; ruled in 8-pt solid; in 9-pt matter both open and ruled set in 8-pt solid; in 8-pt matter open in 6-pt leaded, ruled in 6-pt solid; in 6-pt matter both open and ruled in 6-pt solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growing practice to use different type in tables for totals, averages, percentages; italic and black-face figures may be used to set off classes of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table captions and box-heads styling
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions for columns of open tables and box-heads for ruled tables should ordinarily be set in 6-pt. In ruled tables with multi-story box-heads, upper story (primary heads) in caps and small caps (except when second story is figures only); lower in caps and lower-case. Wherever small caps used in box-heads, the stub (first column) head should also be in caps and small caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of box-head hierarchy and typographic choices; see specimen tables for illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spacing inside ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In ruled tables there should be at least two leads' space between horizontal rules and the matter enclosed, and if practicable at least the equivalent of an en-quad of the body type between perpendicular rules and enclosed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures readability and proper padding within table cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leaders and periods in open and ruled tables
rubrics_metrics.description: In open tables either periods (one em apart and aligned) or leaders may be used between columns. In ruled tables, leaders should usually be used in the stub if there is room. In columns of figures expressing a blank, use leaders the width of the largest number; center figures in the column; if exact centering impossible leave more space on the left than right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition of a leader and rules for the number of dots (each em contains two dots; use at least two dots).

rubrics_metrics.name: Alignment of reading-matter in table columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is reading matter in the columns of a ruled table, it should be centered if possible; if any line runs over, use hanging indention and align all lines on the left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical alignment instruction for multi-line entries in table cells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double rules and table rules conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Double rules should be used at the top of all tables; vertical double rules usually used only when a table is doubled up on itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: tables of two columns should be open; three or more as ruled; 'Table I' headlines set in caps of type used in body of table; descriptive line in caps and small caps; single descriptive headline set in caps of table type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: examples and specimen data formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Specimen tables provided as illustration of recommended formatting for numeric data columns, multi-story box-heads, and distribution tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative samples of table layouts, column alignment, numeric formatting, and measurement annotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point system (typographical unit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The point is the underlying unit of all typographical measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduces the typographic measurement system to be used for sizing and leading tables and other matter (see following rules).
